data.instructions:
Tutorial 2/7:
Minor vs Major errors:
Every error span you mark must be assigned one of two severity levels:
Minor:The meaning is essentially preserved. A reader would notice the translation is slightly awkward or imprecise, but would still understand the message correctly. Minor errors include small word choice differences, minor grammar issues, or slight shifts in tone that do not change the core meaning.
Major:The meaning is changed, lost, or seriously misleading. The reader could misunderstand the intent or act on wrong information. Major errors include hallucinated translation, reversed meanings, dropped key information, or incorrect numbers.
Once you detect an error, click on the beginning and end of the span to mark it as a minor or major error. You will have the above short description of minor and major errors during the annotation.

Now let's try an example:
The word "drama" is incorrect in the following translation. The Estonian word "teatrit" means "theatre" not "drama".
This is a Minor error: the meaning is fully preserved, it is just a small word choice issue.
1. Select and mark the word "drama" as a Minor error.
2. Move the slider to around 70-80% to reflect the reduced quality.

model-tutorial.warning: Please mark the word "drama" as a minor error (light pink) and set the score to 70-80%.

Using the 0-100 quality score slider:

The slider captures your overall judgment. It is not just a count of errors, but how much those errors hurt the translation quality.

Considering the above guideline on the range of scores, let's mark a major error and set a proper score.

Tutorial 6/7:
Annotating more than one translation for a source text:

Here you are given two translations of the same source. You need to follow the rules from the previous examples and mark the error spans, assign severities, and give a 0–100% score to each translation separately. Remember lower quality translations should be assigned lower scores.
One of the translations is accurate. Set the score to 90-100%.
The other translation has two major errors. The words "rõdul" (balcony) and "alt üles" (from below upward) are translated incorrectly to "floor" and "above downward", respectively. Having two major errors, set the score to 10-20%.

data.src: Aga kui heita pilk ajalukku, siis samas majas tegutsenud koolis on õpetajate või õpilastena töötanud või käinud Friedrich Reinhold Kreutzwald, Friedrich Robert Faehlmann, Juhan Kunder, Kristjan Raud, Ernst Peterson-Särgava jpt, ning just sellele majale heisati 1918. aastal esimesena Rakveres sinimustvalge lipp.

tgt.model-tutorial-A: But if one casts a glance at history, in the school that operated in this same building, Friedrich Reinhold Kreutzwald, Friedrich Robert Faehlmann, Juhan Kunder, Kristjan Raud, Ernst Peterson-Särgava and many others worked or studied as teachers or pupils, and it was on this very building, now a protected national monument, that the blue-black-white flag was first raised in Rakvere in 1918.

Tutorial 7/7:
Document-level annotation

In some cases you are given multiple source texts from the same document. While annotating each target text, keep in mind the dependencies across source texts when identifying error spans.

Now let's walk through the following example. In one translation, "now a protected national monument" is a hallucinated phrase that does not appear in the source text. Mark the entire phrase as a major error span and set the score to 0. In the second translation, "esimesena" is mistakenly translated as "last".
